title: Forces
standard_text: Newton's three laws of motion; free-body diagrams and net force; mass, weight and the gravitational field strength; static and kinetic friction and the coefficient of friction; and applying forces in everyday situations. (summary of The Ontario Curriculum, Grades 11 and 12: Science (2008), Physics, Grade 11, University Preparation (SPH3U), Strand C: Forces)
meta_desc: Free Grade 11 Physics (SPH3U) worksheets on forces: Newton's laws, net force and free-body diagrams, weight, friction and the coefficient of friction, and action–reaction pairs. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Fnet = ma: the net force decides the acceleration.
body_html:
How to think about it

Newton's first law: an object keeps its velocity unless a net force acts. Second law: Fnet = ma. Third law: forces come in pairs that are equal in size, opposite in direction and act on different objects.

Draw a free-body diagram, add the forces as vectors and use Fnet = ma. Weight Fg = mg with g = 9.8 N/kg on Earth. Friction opposes sliding: Ff = μFN, with static friction usually larger than kinetic friction.

Example

A 1200 kg car accelerates at 2.5 m/s². Net force?

F = ma = 1200 × 2.5

Answer: 3000 N

Example

A 20 kg box on a horizontal floor, μk = 0.30. Kinetic friction?

FN = 20 × 9.8 = 196 N

Ff = 0.30 × 196

Answer: 58.8 N

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a moving object needs a net force to keep moving at constant speed.
  • Putting both forces of an action–reaction pair on the same object.
  • Confusing mass (kg) with weight (N).

faq.q: Why do you lurch forward when a bus brakes?
faq.a: Your body keeps moving forward (inertia) while the bus slows down.

faq.q: Is the normal force always equal to the weight?
faq.a: Only on flat, horizontal ground with no other vertical forces; on a ramp or in an accelerating elevator it is different.
